blocks.label: First and last
blocks.rationale: Positions in a sequence, going ahead of others, and first-ever experiences. These are the words for explaining steps, taking turns and telling stories.
blocks.interference: saisho and saigo differ only in the ending (sho = start, go = end). hajimete means first-ever, not first in order, and mazu opens a plan. saki ni puts you ahead of someone or something else: mazu tabeyou = let's eat first (step one of a plan), saki ni tabete ii? = can I start eating before you?

items.use: Puts one person or action ahead of another (saki ni itte = go on ahead; saki ni shukudai yaru = I'll do my homework first) or says something is done in advance (saki ni harau = pay up front). Casual speech often drops the ni.

example.english: Mind if I go ahead and start eating?

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni tabete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 先に食べてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Is it all right if I go ahead and start eating?

items.notes: Don't mix it up with sakki (A6, a moment ago): only the double k differs. saki ni kaetta = went home before the others; sakki kaetta = went home a moment ago. 'Before him' is kare yori saki ni, since kare no mae ni usually means 'in front of him'. saki ni itte yo (先に言ってよ) = you should've said so sooner! It sounds the same as saki ni itte (先に行って, go on ahead), so context decides. osaki ni douzo = after you; osaki ni shitsurei shimasu = the set line for leaving work before others.

blocks.label: Soon, suddenly, gradually
blocks.rationale: How soon something happens, from right away to 'it's about time', plus whether a change comes out of the blue or bit by bit.
blocks.interference: sugu = right after, mou sugu = the event is close, sorosoro = it's time (mostly to leave), kyuu ni = without warning, usually in past tense. dandan is the opposite of kyuu ni: the same change spread out, usually with -te kita (dandan samuku natte kita vs kyuu ni samuku natta).

items.use: Says a state changes bit by bit. It almost always pairs with -ku naru / -ni naru, plus -te kita for change up to now (dandan wakatte kita = it's slowly starting to make sense) or -te iku for change from now on (dandan samuku natte iku). Learn natte kita (has been getting) as a chunk here; the -te kuru pattern itself comes later (I-te-kuru).

example.ja: だんだん寒くなってきたね。
example.english: It's been gradually getting colder, hasn't it?

examplePolite.ja: だんだん寒くなってきましたね。
examplePolite.english: It's been gradually getting colder, hasn't it?

items.notes: dandan is for a change in degree (getting colder, getting used to it), not for doing something in small portions. For that, use sukoshi zutsu (sukoshi zutsu tabete, sukoshi zutsu oboeru). For 'slowly' as a speed (speak slowly), use yukkuri.

blocks.label: How often
blocks.rationale: The frequency scale for habits, plus nando mo for one thing repeated again and again. Every one of these goes ahead of the verb phrase it describes.
blocks.interference: Keep the habit words on one scale: itsumo > yoku > tokidoki > tama ni. mainichi literally means every day, not 'always'. nando mo sits off the scale: it counts repeats of one thing, usually in past tense (nando mo itta = I said it over and over), and 'many times' is nando mo, not takusan.

items.use: Says the same thing happened again and again, usually in past tense (nando mo mita = I've seen it loads of times), often with a note of frustration.

example.english: I've told you so many times!

examplePolite.romaji: nando mo itta ja nai desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: 何度も言ったじゃないですか。
examplePolite.english: I've told you so many times!

items.notes: nankai mo means the same and is just as common in casual chat (nankai mo itta jan). ichido mo + negative means 'not even once'. Don't mishear nandemo (anything): nandemo ii = anything's fine.

blocks.label: Not at all / not much
blocks.rationale: The negative-degree scale: each sets how strong a 'no' is before a negative verb or adjective, from zenzen 'not at all' to sonna ni 'not that much'.
blocks.interference: zenzen means 'not at all', hotondo 'hardly' and anmari 'not very'. sonna ni ('not that …') measures against a degree already in the air, either what someone said or what you'd expect, so it often answers a worry or a claim; anmari just rates the thing as low. Without a negative, hotondo flips to 'almost all' and sonna ni to 'so much'.

items.use: Goes before a negative to say 'not as much as you'd think' (sonna ni warukunai = not that bad). Without a negative it means 'so much' (sonna ni tabeta no? = you ate that much?). Said alone, 'e, sonna ni?' reacts to an amount: 'what, that much?', usually surprise, sometimes doubt.

examplePolite.ja: そんなに悪くないですよ
examplePolite.english: It's not that bad.

items.notes: konna ni ('this much', about what's here) and anna ni ('that much', about something you both remember) work the same way: konna ni takusan iranai = I don't need this many; anna ni ganbatta noni = after all that effort. anmari can't do the 'not as much as you imply' job.

blocks.label: Together, alone, as is, without asking
blocks.rationale: Set phrases that give the circumstances of an action (with others, by yourself, leaving things as they are, or without asking anyone), and all fit before a verb like iku.
blocks.interference: issho ni and hitori de share the casual question frame (___ iku?). hitori de is about company and katte ni is about permission: hitori de itchatta (went alone) vs katte ni itchatta (went off without asking). For things that happen by themselves it's katte ni (doa ga katte ni shimatta), not hitori de, which is for people. kono mama is the current situation, often 'if things go on like this'; sono mama is that thing as it stands, or carrying straight on without a further step.

items.english: without asking; as one pleases; by itself (automatically)
items.use: Goes before a verb to say something was done without asking or permission (katte ni kimeta, katte ni tabeta), or that it happened by itself with nobody doing it (doa ga katte ni shimatta). Mostly it's a complaint, but with -te ii it gives free rein (katte ni tabete ii yo = help yourself), and turned on yourself it's an apology (katte ni tsukatte gomen / sumimasen = sorry for using it without asking).

example.english: Don't go deciding things without asking me!

examplePolite.ja: 勝手に決めないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't decide things without asking.

items.freqNote: 勝手に #438; bare 勝手 #756
items.notes: katte ni shite! on its own is a huffy 'suit yourself'. By ear it matches katte from kau (buy), pitch included, so only the ni tells them apart: katte kita (went and bought it) vs katte ni kita (came without being asked). katte from katsu (win) has a different pitch.

blocks.label: Getting through, not wasting a chance
blocks.rationale: Words for handling a situation: start somewhere, push past the details, manage somehow, say how it ended, and don't waste a chance or an effort.
blocks.interference: toriaezu (for now, as a first step) and tonikaku (anyway, whatever else) share '___ yatte miyou'. nantoka is about managing despite trouble; kekkyoku is about the final outcome. sekkaku can't fill that slot on its own. It needs da kara: sekkaku da kara yatte miyou (since we have the chance), never 'sekkaku yatte miyou'. sekkaku ... noni (after all that trouble) often leads into kekkyoku: sekkaku tsukutta noni, kekkyoku tabenakatta (I went to the trouble of making it, and in the end they didn't eat it).

items.english: since we have the chance; after all that trouble
items.use: Marks a chance or an effort as too good to waste, so it only fits something rare or effortful, never a plain 'since'. sekkaku da kara (since we have the chance) and sekkaku kita n da kara (since we came all this way) suggest making the most of it, sekkaku ... noni (after all that trouble) complains that it went to waste, and sekkaku no + noun means 'rare, long-awaited' (sekkaku no yasumi, my rare day off).

example.ja: せっかくだから、やってみよう。
example.english: Since we've got the chance, let's give it a go.

examplePolite.ja: せっかくですから、やってみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Since we have the chance, let's give it a try.

items.freqNote: せっかく #465 (kanji 折角 #47246)
items.notes: A polite way to turn down an offer: sekkaku desu kedo, kyou wa chotto... (that's kind of you, but today's a bit...).

blocks.label: Like & dislike
blocks.rationale: The ways to say how you feel about a thing, from love through like to dislike and can't stand; all can take the X ga ___ frame.
blocks.interference: kirai is a settled dislike of a thing or person; iya is a gut rejection, 'I don't want this / this is unpleasant', usually about what is happening now. Drill 'ame no hi, kirai' (rainy days in general) against 'mata ame? iya da naa' (the rain today). iya also sounds like the interjection iya ('no / well', G): the interjection is soft and opens a reply (iya, chigau yo), while the adjective is emphatic and stands alone or ends the sentence (iya!, iya da, iya na yokan). daisuki is just a stronger suki (dai- = big) on the same rainy-days sentence, so add it once suki is solid.

items.use: A stronger suki for food, hobbies and places, in the same X ga ___ frame; like suki it is a na-adjective (daisuki ja nai, daisuki datta). About family, kids or pets it is warm, but daisuki (desu) said to one person's face means 'I love you'.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no hi ga daisuki desu
examplePolite.ja: 雨の日が大好きです
examplePolite.english: I love rainy days.

items.freqNote: 大好き #579
items.notes: dai- works on kirai too: daikirai = really hate.

blocks.label: Glad, let down, worried
blocks.rationale: Your own emotional reactions to news and to what's coming: glad, disappointed, looking forward, scared, worried.
blocks.interference: kowai (scared) and shinpai (worried) share the exam-results sentence so only the feeling changes, and ureshii and zannen are paired replies to news. kowai also sounds like kawaii (cute, earlier block): three beats against four. tanoshimi (looking forward to it) is not tanoshii (fun, earlier block): say ryokou, tanoshimi before the trip and ryokou, tanoshikatta after it.

items.use: Says you're looking forward to something coming up, as a one-word reply to any plan (tanoshimi!) or X ga tanoshimi; it is a noun, so it takes da / desu, and tanoshimi ni shiteru is the fuller 'I'm looking forward to it'.

examplePolite.ja: 旅行、楽しみですね
examplePolite.english: I'm looking forward to the trip.

items.freqNote: 楽しみ #869
items.notes: Politely, tanoshimi ni shitemasu is the set phrase for 'I'm looking forward to it'.

blocks.label: Hot, cold, ouch
blocks.rationale: How the weather and your body feel: hot, cold and it hurts, the daily small-talk openers and the reports you have to make on the spot.
blocks.interference: atsui and samui are opposites with the same shape (three beats ending -ui) on the same sentence (kyou, ___ ne), so learn atsui first; per 11-list-adjectives note 9(a), keep samui at least 10 items after atsui in drill order even though they share a block. atsui covers hot air and hot things, but samui is only for the air and how you feel: a cold drink is tsumetai. itai (it hurts) sounds almost the same as iru + -tai (want to stay): atama ga itai vs zutto koko ni itai, and the words before it tell you which.

items.use: Says it's hot, about the weather and air (kyou atsui ne) or about food, drinks and things you touch; the top small-talk opener in summer. Written 暑い for weather and 熱い for things, but it is one word by ear.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は暑いですね
examplePolite.english: It's hot today.

items.freqNote: 熱い #1030 (hot to the touch / passionate); 暑い #1990 (weather). Same sound for both.
items.notes: Touching something hot, people clip it to atsu!; atsui 'thick' differs only in pitch.

items.use: Says it's cold, about the weather and how you feel (samui! = I'm cold); not for cold drinks or objects, which are tsumetai.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は寒いですね
examplePolite.english: It's cold today.

items.notes: Often clipped to samu!; the drawled samii! is rough, mostly male speech. samui also means a joke fell flat.

items.use: Reports pain (atama ga itai = my head hurts; doko ga itai? = where does it hurt?) and is the reflex 'ouch!'; figuratively, sore wa itai = that hurts, that's a blow.

example.english: I've got a bit of a headache.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと頭が痛いです
examplePolite.english: I've got a bit of a headache.

items.notes: As a reflex it is clipped to ita! or stretched to ittaa!; itee! / ite! are rough and masculine. About a person or behaviour (ano hito, itai) it is slang for 'cringey'.

blocks.label: New, pretty, kind, skilled
blocks.rationale: What you notice and praise about people and their things: new, pretty or clean, kind, good at something.
blocks.interference: kirei (pretty, clean; said kiree) is close by ear to kirai (hate, earlier block): per 11-list-adjectives keep kirei at least 12 items after kirai, and listen for the pitch, since KI-ree falls after the first beat while ki-RAI rises and stays up. kirei is beautiful or clean while kawaii (earlier block) is cute: a sunset is kirei, a puppy kawaii. yasashii here is only 'kind'; for 'easy' say kantan (earlier block).

items.use: Says something is new: things you've bought, a job, a shop, a phone, news; it goes straight before a noun (atarashii shigoto).

examplePolite.ja: その服、新しいですか？
examplePolite.english: Is that outfit new?

items.freqNote: 新しい #301
items.notes: Its opposite furui (old) means not new and never describes a person's age: furui tomodachi is a long-time friend. For age, say toshiue (older than me).

items.use: Says something looks lovely or is clean and tidy: views, places, people, rooms, handwriting; kirei ni makes it an adverb (kirei ni shite = tidy it up).

examplePolite.ja: 海がきれいですね
examplePolite.english: The sea is beautiful.

items.notes: Said kiree; a na-adjective despite the -i: kirei ja nai, kirei datta (never kireikunai).

items.use: Describes a kind or gentle person or act; after arigatou, yasashii ne compliments someone for a kindness they just did.

example.english: Thanks, that's so kind of you.

examplePolite.ja: ありがとうございます、優しいですね
examplePolite.english: Thank you, that's so kind of you.

items.freqNote: 優しい #419; 易しい 'easy' #45300 (kantan covers 'easy')
alsoIn: vocab-trainer core-vocab: i-adjectives (carded there as 'easy', the other yasashii)
items.notes: A separate yasashii means 'easy'; use kantan for that and keep this card for 'kind'. yasashii desu ne suits peers and people you know well; to a stranger, boss or teacher who helps you, say arigatou gozaimasu, tasukarimashita instead.

items.use: Compliments someone else's skill: X ga jouzu (you're good at X), or jouzu da ne after watching them; jouzu ni = well, skilfully. About yourself, use it only in the negative or as a goal (mada jouzu ja nai, jouzu ni naritai): claiming it sounds like boasting.

blocks.label: Depends / without / for / so that
blocks.rationale: Linkers that do the job of an English preposition or 'so that': depends on X, without doing X, in order to / for X, so that (not) X.
blocks.interference: -naide (without) vs -nakute (because not). -tame ni (purpose, an action you choose) vs -you ni (so that): after potentials and verbs you don't control only you ni sounds right (hanaseru you ni, maniau you ni, not hanaseru tame ni); after -nai, you ni is the everyday choice (wasurenai you ni) and -nai tame ni sounds stiff. Listen around it: noun + no you ni is 'like' (yume no you ni), itta you ni is 'like I said', and you ni naru / you ni iu mean 'come to' / 'tell someone to'; they all sound the same.

items.english: so that; so as not to
items.use: Plain verb + you ni gives a purpose you can't directly control: after potentials (hanaseru you ni), non-volitional verbs like kikoeru and maniau, or when the purpose is someone else's state (minna ga wakaru you ni), where tame ni doesn't fit; after -nai forms it's the everyday choice (wasurenai you ni). The polite form goes on the main verb.

example.ja: 忘れないように書いとくね。
example.english: I'll write it down so I don't forget.

examplePolite.romaji: wasurenai you ni kaite okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 忘れないように書いておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll write it down so I don't forget.

items.freqNote: ように #158, which also counts the simile 'like' and 'as' (itta you ni); ようになる #462 and ようにする #903 are separate entries
items.notes: At the end of a sentence it's a reminder or wish: 'kaze hikanai you ni ne' = 'don't catch a cold, OK?'; polite: 'kaze o hikanai you ni ki o tsukete kudasai ne'. As a set wish it keeps -masu even with friends: 'umaku ikimasu you ni' = 'here's hoping it goes well'. A different you ni: 'mae mo itta you ni' = 'like I said before'.

blocks.label: More enders
blocks.rationale: Four endings built on items you already have: -te plus ne for a friendly ask, n da plus yo for an insistent reason, darou, the plain form of deshou, for wondering aloud, and -tara plus ii na for hoping.
blocks.interference: darou is the plain deshou, but in casual speech only its wondering uses (nan darou, daijoubu darou ka) are neutral, so say kamo for 'probably' and desho? for 'right?'. n da yo pushes a reason across where n da just explains, and -te ne assumes a yes where -te kurenai? asks. ikitai na wants to do it yourself; iketara ii na hopes you'll get the chance, and haretara ii na hopes for something out of your hands. Swap na for yo and it becomes advice (kiitara ii yo = you should ask).

items.english: I hope / I wish / it'd be nice if
items.use: Hopes for something you can't simply do yourself, like weather, results or someone else's choice: add ii na to a -tara clause (haretara ii na = I hope it's sunny). With a potential verb it hopes you'll get the chance (iketara ii na = I hope I can go; mata aetara ii ne = hope we can meet again), and about something that isn't so it means 'I wish' (okane ga attara ii na = I wish I had money). ii na is half to yourself; -tara ii ne and polite -tara ii desu ne share the hope with the listener, and -nakattara ii na hopes something won't happen.

example.ja: 一緒に行けたらいいな
example.english: I hope we can go together.

blocks.label: Thanks, sorry, please
blocks.rationale: The everyday politeness formulas for thanking, apologising, asking and offering, plus kochira koso, which hands thanks or an apology straight back.
blocks.interference: sumimasen apologises and also thanks, while gomen only apologises. onegai is 'please' when you ask for something; douzo is 'please' when you offer it. kochira koso doesn't mean 'you're welcome': it returns the same thanks, apology or yoroshiku to the speaker.

items.use: Returns whatever the other person just said, whether thanks, an apology or yoroshiku, and is usually followed by that same word.

example.ja: こちらこそ、ありがとうね。

examplePolite.ja: こちらこそ、ありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: No, thank YOU.

items.freqNote: こちらこそ #1155; casual こっちこそ has no entry because the tokenizer splits it into こっち #148 + こそ #320, so no rank
items.notes: Friends also say kotchi koso. To yoroshiku, answer kochira koso yoroshiku (onegai shimasu). It isn't 'me too': to say you feel or do the same, use watashi mo.

blocks.label: Phrases for occasions
blocks.rationale: Fixed phrases tied to a particular moment: meals, bedtime, the end of shared work, and seeing someone again.
blocks.interference: itadakimasu comes before eating and gochisousama after. oyasumi and otsukare are both sign-offs: oyasumi for the night, otsukare after work or study together. hisashiburi greets someone you're meeting again and is never a goodbye.

items.use: Said just before you start eating or drinking, alone or with others. It's already a -masu form, so every register uses it unchanged.

example.ja: うわ、おいしそう！いただきます！

examplePolite.ja: おいしそうですね。いただきます。
examplePolite.english: That looks delicious. Thank you, I'll dig in.

items.freqNote: いただきます #486; 頂きます #2378
items.notes: Also accepts something offered, like a drink or a sweet: jaa, itadakimasu = 'don't mind if I do'.

items.use: Said when you finish eating, and to whoever cooked or paid. To a host or someone who treated you, use gochisousama deshita.

example.ja: ああ、おいしかった！ごちそうさま！
example.english: Ah, that was good! Thanks for the meal!

examplePolite.ja: おいしかったです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: That was delicious. Thank you for the meal.

items.freqNote: ごちそうさま #2052; polite ごちそうさまでした #1827
items.notes: At a restaurant, gochisousama deshita on the way out is the usual thank-you to the staff.

items.use: Said when going to bed, parting late at night, or ending a night-time call or chat. It's only a goodbye, never a greeting.

example.ja: じゃあ、また明日。おやすみ。

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、また明日。おやすみなさい。
examplePolite.english: Well, see you tomorrow. Good night.

items.freqNote: おやすみ #1575; polite おやすみなさい #2270 (お休み #1980 also counts the 'day off' sense)
items.notes: yasumi means 'day off, break', and its polite version is also oyasumi: ashita yasumi = 'I'm off tomorrow'; ashita oyasumi desu ka? = 'are you off tomorrow?'. oyasumi means 'good night' only at bedtime or when parting at night.

items.use: Said to people you work or study with when you finish something together or part for the day. With seniors say otsukaresama desu, or otsukaresama deshita once the work is over.

example.romaji: jaa, kyou wa koko made ni shiyou. otsukare!
example.ja: じゃあ、今日はここまでにしよう。お疲れ！
example.english: Okay, let's call it a day. Good work!

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, kyou wa koko made ni shimashou. otsukaresama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、今日はここまでにしましょう。お疲れさまでした。
examplePolite.english: Well, let's stop here for today. Thanks for all your work.

items.freqNote: お疲れ #848; お疲れさま #504
items.notes: Comes from tsukareru (get tired). At work it is also a passing 'hi' and the reply to someone who leaves first.

items.use: Greets someone you haven't seen or talked to in a while. It also marks doing something again after a long gap.

example.english: Long time no see! How've you been?

examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お元気でしたか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a long time. How have you been?

items.freqNote: 久しぶり #594; polite お久しぶり #1495
items.notes: hisashiburi ni + verb means 'for the first time in ages': hisashiburi ni sushi tabeta.

blocks.label: Comfort and cheer
blocks.rationale: What you say back to someone's news: relief, a shrug, encouragement, denying a put-down, and congratulations.
blocks.interference: yokatta looks like a past tense but is relief you feel right now; it says you're glad, while omedetou congratulates the person (people often say both). shouganai accepts a bad outcome, while sonna koto nai rejects a negative claim.

items.politeJa: おめでとうございます
items.use: Congratulates someone on good news, a birthday or the new year. The occasion goes in front: tanjoubi omedetou.

example.ja: 結婚するんだ！おめでとう！

examplePolite.romaji: kekkon suru n desu ka. omedetou gozaimasu!
examplePolite.ja: 結婚するんですか。おめでとうございます！
examplePolite.english: Oh, you're getting married! Congratulations!

items.freqNote: おめでとう #774; polite おめでとうございます #1249
items.notes: For the new year, say akemashite omedetou (gozaimasu). It often comes with yokatta: yokatta ne, omedetou!

blocks.label: Be, have, live
blocks.rationale: The ways to say something is there or that you have it — aru for things, iru for people and animals, motteru for what you own or carry — plus sumu for where you live.
blocks.interference: aru vs iru depends on whether the thing is alive (kasa aru / neko iru), and that holds for 'have' too: kyoudai iru? / inu iru? but jikan aru?; motteru is for what's in your possession or on you (kasa motteru?); iru is where you are now and sunderu where you live (ima doko ni iru? / doko ni sunderu?).

items.use: Says where someone lives, with the place marked by ni; your current home takes the -teru form (doko ni sunderu?), the plain form is for a move ahead (rainen toukyou ni sumu) and -tai for a wish (toukyou ni sumitai).

examplePolite.ja: どこに住んでますか？
examplePolite.english: Where do you live?

items.freqNote: 住む #548; homophone 済む (be over) #671 and kana-written すむ #1535 are separate entries
items.notes: Homophone sumu 'be over, be settled' (済む) also gives sunde, sunda, and its polite negative is sumimasen (sorry), one sound off sumimasu; for where you live now say sundemasu, and 'I don't live there' is sundenai / sundemasen.

blocks.label: Do, can, become, change
blocks.rationale: The structural action verbs — do (suru, casual yaru), can do (dekiru) and become (naru) — that turn nouns and adjectives into events, plus kawaru for something changing on its own.
blocks.interference: suru and yaru overlap as 'do' (nani shiteru / nani yatteru), but only suru builds noun+suru verbs (shinpai suru, renraku suru); 'can do' for those is X dekiru, not a potential form of suru; naru says what something became (samuku natta) while kawaru says it's different from before (kawatta ne) and names the result only with ni (yotei ga raishuu ni kawatta); its transitive partner kaeru (change it) gives kaeta (changed it), one doubled t away from kaetta (went home).

items.use: Says something changed on its own (a person, plan, place or price), with the thing marked by ga; changing it yourself is the transitive kaeru (kaeta).

examplePolite.ja: 変わってませんね。
examplePolite.english: You haven't changed.

items.freqNote: 変わる #226; 代わる (take over, swap) #1244 counted separately
items.notes: kawatteru / kawatta often means odd or unusual, not 'is changing' (kawatteru ne = you're a bit unusual; kawatta hito = an odd person). 代わる shares the sound: kawarou ka? = want me to take over?

blocks.label: Knowing and learning
blocks.rationale: Verbs for what you know: understand, know, remember, forget, and study — the ones a learner uses about themselves in every exchange.
blocks.interference: wakaranai = I can't understand or work it out, shiranai = I have no information — but when you just can't answer a question (a stranger asks the way), wakarimasen / wakannai is the soft default and shirimasen sounds curt. 'Remember' is oboeteru, not shitteru; both live in the -teru form. oboeru is fixing a fact in memory and benkyou suru is putting in study time (tango oboeta / nihongo benkyou shiteru).

items.use: Says you study something, with o often dropped in casual speech (nihongo benkyou shiteru); benkyou ni naru (that's good to know) is the stock reply to an explanation.

example.ja: 日本語勉強してるんだ。

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo o benkyou shiteru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 日本語を勉強してるんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm studying Japanese.

items.freqNote: 勉強する is not a separate entry; rank of 勉強 #729
items.notes: benkyou ni narimashita thanks someone for teaching you something.

blocks.label: Think, feel, mind
blocks.rationale: Verbs for what's going on in your head: an opinion (omou), thinking it over (kangaeru), something on your mind (ki ni naru), a hunch (ki ga suru), minding it (ki ni suru) and taking care (ki o tsukeru).
blocks.interference: omou gives a view (... to omou) while kangaeru means working something through (mada kangaeteru); ki ga suru (a hunch, takes a clause) and ki ni naru (it nags at me, takes ga) share ki but differ in particle and verb; ki ni naru (it bothers me) and ki ni suru (I let it bother me) are an intransitive/transitive pair, heard mostly as ki ni naru and ki ni shinaide; ki o tsukete (take care) is the one with o, said at goodbyes.

items.use: Says someone minds or worries about something, with the thing marked by o; mostly heard as ki ni shinaide (don't worry about it) after an apology or thanks, and ki ni shinai (I don't mind).

example.english: It's fine, don't worry about it.

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu yo, ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: いいですよ、気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: It's fine, don't worry about it.

items.freqNote: 気にする #725 as a lexicalized entry
items.notes: Also mada ki ni shiteru no? = are you still worried about that?

items.use: Means paying attention so nothing goes wrong; ki o tsukete (take care, get home safe) is a standard goodbye, and ki o tsukemasu (I'll be careful) answers a warning or closes your own apology (sumimasen, kondo kara ki o tsukemasu).

examplePolite.romaji: ki o tsukete kaette kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 気をつけて帰ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Get home safe.

items.freqNote: 気をつける #1226; 気をつけて #1735 and 気を付ける #2218 counted separately
items.notes: The danger takes ni: kuruma ni ki o tsukete = watch out for cars.

blocks.label: Start, stop, keep at it
blocks.rationale: Phases of an activity — something starting (hajimaru) or you starting it (hajimeru), its ending, quitting it — plus ganbaru, the effort of keeping at it.
blocks.interference: owatta = it finished (shigoto owatta, done for the day) while yameta = someone stopped or quit (shigoto yameta, quit the job); hajimaru (it starts, ga) vs hajimeru (you start it, o): eiga ga hajimaru / shigoto o hajimeru.

items.use: Says an event, class, show or season starts, with it marked by ga; starting something yourself is hajimeru with o.

examplePolite.ja: 何時から始まりますか？
examplePolite.english: What time does it start?

items.freqNote: 始まる #435
items.notes: mou hajimatteru = it's already started.

blocks.label: Give, get, lend, help
blocks.rationale: The giving triad, where direction picks the verb: away from me (ageru), toward me (kureru), I receive (morau) — plus lending (kasu) and helping (tetsudau), the favours that ride on it.
blocks.interference: ageru and kureru both translate 'give' but point opposite ways — anything coming to me or my side is kureru; morau makes the receiver the subject and marks the giver with ni; kashite means 'lend me' (the other person lends), while borrowing from your side is kariru (karite ii?); tetsudau is help with a task, the cry for help is tasukete.

items.use: Helps someone with a task, with the person or the task marked by o; later forms build on it: nanka tetsudaou ka? offers help and tetsudatte kureru? asks for it.

example.ja: 明日の引っ越し、手伝うよ。

examplePolite.ja: 明日の引っ越し、手伝いますよ。
examplePolite.english: I'll help you move tomorrow.

items.freqNote: 手伝う #508
items.notes: tasukete! is the cry for help; tetsudatte is for a hand with a task.

items.use: Lends something, with the borrower marked by ni; kashite (lend me) is the everyday way to ask to borrow or use a pen, a charger or a shop's bathroom.

example.english: Can I borrow a pen for a sec?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ペン貸してください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could I borrow a pen?

items.freqNote: 貸す #658; 借りる (borrow) #673
items.notes: kashite is learned here as a chunk; the -te request itself comes in F4. Borrowing is kariru (ichidan): karite ii? = can I borrow it?, karita = borrowed.

blocks.label: Take, put out, cost, call
blocks.rationale: Wide-reach light verbs whose meaning comes from the object: toru (take, pass, get), dasu (put out, take out, hand in, pay), kakaru (time or money it takes), kakeru (cause trouble, call, spend, put on).
blocks.interference: 'It takes an hour' is kakaru, not toru; kakaru (it takes, ga) and kakeru (spend, call, o) are an intransitive/transitive pair — jikan ga kakaru vs jikan o kakeru; dasu is likewise the transitive partner of deru: uchi o deta (I left home) vs gomi o dashita (I put the trash out).

items.english: put out; take out; hand in; pay
items.use: Puts or takes something out, with it marked by o (gomi dasu, saifu dasu, shukudai dasu), covers paying (kyou wa watashi ga dasu yo = I'll get this today), and builds set phrases like genki dashite (cheer up) and koe dasu (speak up).

example.english: Did you put the trash out this morning?

examplePolite.ja: 今朝ゴミを出しましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you put the trash out this morning?

items.notes: After a verb stem it means 'start to': ame ga furidashita = it started raining.

blocks.label: Meeting up
blocks.rationale: The verbs of the day itself: hanging out, getting there, running late.
blocks.interference: tsuku is arriving, not coming (ima iku, mou sugu tsuku, tsuita); asobu is hanging out, never playing a sport (tenisu suru); okureta (was late) and okutta (sent) differ by one sound.

items.use: Means spending free time for fun, kids playing or adults hanging out (tomodachi to asobu); asobou is the casual invite and asobi ni kite means 'come over'.

examplePolite.ja: 今度遊びましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's get together sometime.

items.notes: Playing a sport or game is suru (tenisu suru, geemu suru); piano or guitar is hiku.

items.use: Says someone gets to a place, marked by ni (eki ni tsuita), and carries the meet-up messages: mou sugu tsuku, tsuita yo, tsuitara renraku shite.

example.english: I just got to the station.

examplePolite.ja: 今駅に着きました。
examplePolite.english: I've just arrived at the station.

items.freqNote: 着く #957; kana-written つく #355 can't be split by sense and is mostly the 付く/点く senses (come on, stick); 付く #1570 is a separate entry
items.notes: Homophone tsuku 'come on, stick' (付く/点く): denki ga tsuita = the light came on.

items.use: Says someone or something is late for a set time or behind schedule, with the event marked by ni (kaigi ni okureta); okurete gomen is the apology on arrival and densha okureteru (the train's delayed) the standard excuse.

example.ja: ごめん、10分ぐらい遅れる。
example.english: Sorry, I'll be about ten minutes late.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、10分ぐらい遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'll be about ten minutes late.

items.freqNote: 遅れる #955
items.notes: A friend complaining you're late says osoi!; okureta is the explanation.

blocks.label: Favours and passive
blocks.rationale: The giving/receiving triad that marks who benefits from an action, the everyday thanks built on kureru, and the passive for things done to you, often unwanted.
blocks.interference: Same act, three viewpoints: tomodachi ga oshiete kureta / tomodachi ni oshiete moratta / tomodachi ni oshiete ageta. Kureru points toward the speaker, ageru away, and morau takes the receiver's view with the giver on ni. The passive keeps that ni frame, often for something unwanted: tomodachi ni tetsudatte moratta (glad) vs tomodachi ni okorareta (not glad), so a favour takes -te morau, not the passive. The ichidan passive sounds like the I3 potential (taberareru = can eat / gets eaten), while godan keeps them apart (ieru / iwareru); casual potentials often drop the ra (tabereru), passives never do. When you thank someone for an act, keep the kureru: oshiete kurete arigatou, never oshiete arigatou or oshiete agete arigatou.

items.politeJa: 〜てくれてありがとうございます
items.use: Thanks someone for one specific thing they did for you. It goes on any verb's -te form (kite, tetsudatte, oshiete), and the kureru is what makes the act a favour to you.

example.ja: 今日は来てくれてありがとう。

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kite kurete arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は来てくれてありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: Thanks for coming today.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; rank of kana くれる, the rarer part (ありがとう alone #128), so an upper bound
items.notes: Uses the same -te + feeling frame as okurete gomen (sorry I'm late) and kite yokatta (glad I came). Politely, once the act is over and you're parting, the past is usual: kite kurete arigatou gozaimashita.

items.use: Puts you on the receiving end of what someone did, with the doer on ni. The everyday one is iwareta, reporting what someone told you (isha ni yasume tte iwareta); many others are unwelcome (okorareta, ame ni furareta). Godan verbs change -u to -areru (okoru -> okorareru; after a vowel, -u becomes -wareru: iu -> iwareru), ichidan verbs swap -ru for -rareru (taberu -> taberareru), and the irregulars are sareru and korareru.

example.english: A friend got mad at me yesterday.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日友達に怒られました。
examplePolite.english: A friend got mad at me yesterday.

items.freqNote: rank of the auxiliary られる, which also counts ichidan potential and honorific -rareru; れる #3142, される #22435; the tokenizer splits most passives off the verb (言われる, 怒られる not found as wholes), a few keep their own entry (呼ばれる #2851)
items.notes: It even works on verbs that take no object, for being put out (ame ni furareta = got caught in the rain), and keeps o for something of yours (saifu o torareta = got my wallet taken). Don't use it for English 'got broken' or 'was left open': Japanese uses the intransitive verb (keitai kowarechatta, mado ga aiteru), and kowasareta says someone broke it. The ichidan passive sounds the same as the full potential (taberareru), so context decides; casual speech often shortens the potential to tabereru, so a full -rareru in casual talk leans passive.

blocks.label: Me, us, home
blocks.rationale: Beyond watashi: boku, the softer male 'I' that works casually and with desu/masu, -tachi for 'we' and 'X and the others', and uchi for home and 'our side'.
blocks.interference: boku is for men only; it is fine with desu/masu among coworkers, but watashi is safer with strangers and superiors. -tachi goes on people, never on things. uchi ni (at home) sounds like -uchi ni (while), which follows a verb, an adjective or X no (atsui uchi ni, kyou no uchi ni).

items.use: The softer male 'I': gentle among friends (ore is the rougher, very common one there) and still fine with desu/masu among coworkers. Women don't use it, and with strangers, clients and superiors watashi is the safe choice, so the polite form here is watashi.

examplePolite.ja: 私もそう思います。
examplePolite.english: I think so too.

items.freqNote: 僕 #123; rougher 俺 ore #44
items.notes: ore is the rougher male 'I' among friends: learn to recognise it and save it until you know the group. Adults also call a small boy boku (boku, namae wa? = what's your name?), so there it means 'you'.

items.use: Attaches to a person word or a name to mean that person and their group: watashitachi (we), kodomotachi (the kids), tanaka-san-tachi (Tanaka and the others). It is used for people (and pets), never for things.

example.ja: 田中さんたちはもう帰ったよ。
example.english: Tanaka and the others already went home.

examplePolite.ja: 田中さんたちはもう帰りましたよ。
examplePolite.english: Tanaka and the others already went home.

items.notes: Men also say bokutachi or bokura, and oretachi or orera (rougher, common among male friends). Plural is optional: kodomo alone can already mean 'the kids', so add -tachi when you want to stress the group.

items.use: Means home, usually your own (uchi ni iru, uchi ni kaeru), and uchi no puts the next noun on your side: uchi no kaisha (our company), uchi no ko (my kid).

example.english: Want to come over to my place today?

examplePolite.ja: 今日、うちに来ませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to come over to my place today?

items.freqNote: うち #113, which also counts -uchi ni 'while' (A-uchi-ni); 家 read いえ #152
items.notes: ie means the house as a building. As 'I', uchi is Kansai or young women's speech, so just recognise it.

blocks.label: How / this way
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/do manner words plus dou yatte and dou shita: how something went, how it is done, 'like that', and what's wrong.
blocks.interference: dou asks for an opinion or report (dou datta?), dou yatte asks for the method (dou yatte iku?), and dou shita no? asks what has happened to you; the bare reply sou (sou da ne) is drilled in G, so the so- card here is sou iu.

items.use: The check-in when someone looks upset, hurt or late (dou shita no?); after a noun it asks what became of the thing (kagi dou shita? = what did you do with the key?).

example.romaji: dou shita no? genki nai ne.
example.ja: どうしたの？元気ないね。

examplePolite.romaji: dou shita n desu ka? genki nai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: どうしたんですか？元気ないですね。
examplePolite.english: What's wrong? You seem down.

items.notes: Staff and doctors say dou shimashita ka? to ask what the problem is. Don't mix it up with dou suru? (what will you do?).

blocks.label: In, on, near, other
blocks.rationale: Relational nouns that attach to another noun with no to say where something is (in, on, in front, near) or that it is a different one.
blocks.interference: naka/soto, ue/shita, mae/ushiro and chikaku come after the noun (hako no naka, eki no mae) but hoka comes before (hoka no hito); ue/shita also mean older/younger, and mae also means before/ago in time.

items.use: Places people and things in front or behind (eki no mae, ushiro no seki); X no mae de is the standard way to set a meeting point.

example.romaji: mae ja nakute, ushiro ni aru yo.
example.ja: 前じゃなくて、後ろにあるよ。
example.english: It's not on the front, it's on the back.

examplePolite.romaji: mae ja nakute, ushiro ni arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 前じゃなくて、後ろにありますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's not on the front, it's on the back.

items.freqNote: 前 #80, all senses combined (time sense shared with A-mae); 後ろ ushiro #1090
items.notes: eki no mae de matteru ne = I'll wait in front of the station. In time, the opposite of mae is ato (ato de = later), not ushiro.

items.use: Says something is close by: after a noun + no it means 'near X' (eki no chikaku), and on its own it means 'nearby' (chikaku ni aru, chikaku no mise).

example.romaji: eki no chikaku ni aru yo.

examplePolite.romaji: eki no chikaku ni arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 駅の近くにありますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's near the station.

items.notes: For 'a nearby shop' say chikaku no mise, not chikai mise; chikai + noun mostly comes as ichiban chikai (the nearest). The adjective chikai talks about the distance itself (eki kara chikai = close to the station).
